    14. Dense subclasses of #

    The spaces are complete for every (Notes 25 and 26). A general element of , however, is only an equivalence class of measurable functions, and many statements are easier to verify for functions with additional structure: simple functions take finitely many values, and continuous functions can be evaluated at points and controlled on compact sets. A class of functions is dense in if every element of is an limit of functions from that class. A typical density argument proves a statement for the functions of the class and transfers it to all of by passing to the limit.

    These notes establish two dense classes. We first recall why simple functions whose support has finite measure are dense in for , and we show that this density fails in . We then prove that bounded continuous functions are dense in for every finite Borel measure on a metric space , and we state that compactly supported continuous functions are dense in for every Borel measure on that is finite on compact sets; the proof of this last statement is left to Homework 08. The proof reduces the approximation of a general function to the approximation of the indicator of a single closed set . The regularity of finite Borel measures replaces each Borel set appearing in a simple function by a closed subset of almost the same measure, and the continuous functions , where is the distance from to , converge to in .

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Prove that simple functions with support of finite measure are dense in for , and show that they are not dense in when .

    • State and prove the regularity of finite Borel measures on metric spaces by closed and open sets, and on by compact sets.

    • Approximate the indicator of a closed set in by continuous functions built from the distance to that set.

    • Prove that bounded continuous functions are dense in for every finite Borel measure on a metric space and every .

    • State the density of compactly supported continuous functions in for Borel measures finite on compact sets, and explain why this density fails for some -finite Borel measures and for .

    Throughout these notes, unless is stated explicitly, and functions are measurable functions with values in . A subset is dense in if for every and every there exists with .

    Theorem 14.3 (Density of continuous functions for finite Borel measures)#

    For a finite Borel measure on a metric space and , the set is dense in .

    By Theorem 14.1, it suffices to approximate simple functions, and hence indicators of Borel sets. A continuous function cannot jump from on to outside , so it must make the transition on a region around the boundary of .     14.4 Proof of density#

    The proof of Theorem 14.3 passes through three classes of functions. By Theorem 14.1, every is an limit of simple functions with Borel sets . By inner regularity (Theorem 14.4), each can be replaced by a closed subset of almost the same measure, which yields a simple function whose level sets are closed. Finally, each indicator of a closed set is approximated by continuous functions. In the last two reductions, the quasi-triangle inequality reduces the approximation of a linear combination to the approximation of a single indicator.
